scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4659: The campus network keeps going slow for us in bursts
-- transfers crawl for a bit, then recover, then crawl again, and it is like
that in waves for everyone, not just one desk. A couple of the more
technical people here are certain about it: the main router -- they call it
router0 -- is dropping our packets. I wouldn't know a packet if I saw one,
and I don't have to; they would. Something is losing our traffic and it is
on your side. Check it and sort it out today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0 has ip_forward enabled, its interfaces
  are up, and traffic transiting router0 between segments arrives with 0% loss; there
  is no drop-inducing ACL or forwarding fault. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of packet loss on router0 that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- router0 dropping/forwarding
traffic incorrectly -- is NOT reproducible: a ping across router0 (between two
segments it connects) completes with 0% loss, router0 has ip_forward enabled, its
interfaces are up, ripd is running, and there is no drop-inducing ACL.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: router0 is forwarding correctly and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces a path transiting
router0, finds 0% loss, checks router0's ip_forward, interfaces, and any filters, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" router0 dropping packets -- blaming an ACL,
forwarding, or load to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
A thorough examination of every layer of the Kath2 campus network finds no fault. All three routers (router0, router1, router2) have their RIP daemons running with correct in-memory configuration, their full routing tables populated and stable (last RIP update received within seconds on every peer), and zero bad-packet or bad-route counters. Traffic-control inspection across every interface on every router and switch shows only the default fq_codel qdisc at root, with zero dropped, overlimit, or requeued packets and no child qdiscs, token-bucket filters, or netem rules anywhere in the topology. All iptables filter and mangle chains are empty with ACCEPT default policies. No background scripts, cron jobs, or unusual processes are running on any device. A live reachability test spanning six source/destination pairs across the full network (LAN-office to LAN-principle, LAN-servers, LAN-internet) returns 0% packet loss on every pair with sub-2 ms average RTT.

The symptom described — periodic "waves" of slowness campus-wide attributed to router0 dropping packets — has no matching fault in the live lab. The users' diagnosis appears to be incorrect: router0 shows no queue drops, no iptables filtering, stable RIP adjacency with router1, and correct forwarding of all reachability probes. The most likely explanation is that the perceived slowness was transient and caused by a non-network-layer factor (application load, upstream service delay, etc.), or represents normal variation that users misattributed to the router. The corrective action is to collect timestamped throughput measurements during a future "slow" episode and cross-correlate with server CPU and application logs before concluding any network-layer fault exists.

per_axis.rationale: Agent confirms 0% transit loss but does not explicitly state that router0's ip_forward is enabled and its interfaces are up.
